html:
The Soyombo script is an alphabet for Mongolian created in 1686 by Zanabazar, the first head of Mongolian Buddhism, who was also a sculptor and scholar. Its name is said to come from the Sanskrit svayambhu, "self-created".

Zanabazar based its letters on Indian scripts and designed it to write Mongolian, and also Tibetan and Sanskrit, the languages of Buddhist scripture, more exactly than the old Uyghur-derived Mongolian script. It was used mainly for religious texts and temple inscriptions and never in daily life; it was too complex.

One of its signs lives on. The Soyombo symbol, a column made of fire, sun, moon, triangles, bars and a yin-yang, has been a national emblem of Mongolia since independence in 1911, and it stands on the left of the national flag. Zanabazar also designed a second alphabet, the horizontal square script. Mongolia later switched to the Cyrillic alphabet in 1941.
